## 1. Core Concepts

### 1.1 Concurrency vs Parallelism vs Asynchrony

These three terms are often used interchangeably, but they mean different things.

```
CONCURRENCY   = several operations in progress over the same time span
                (they may take turns on one thread)

PARALLELISM   = several operations literally executing at the same instant
                (needs multiple cores AND something that can use them)

ASYNCHRONY    = an operation that waits without holding a thread
                (I/O: network, disk, timers)
```

```
Concurrent, not parallel (1 thread, interleaved):
  Thread 1:  [A][B][A][C][B][A]

Parallel (multiple cores at once):
  Core 1:    [A A A A A A]
  Core 2:    [B B B B B B]

Asynchronous (waiting costs no thread):
  Thread:    [A start]......(thread runs other tasks meanwhile)......[A resume]
```

| Term        | Meaning                                       | Needs multiple cores? | Typical Python tool                                   |
| ----------- | --------------------------------------------- | --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| Concurrency | Many operations in progress at once           | No                    | `asyncio`, `threading`                                |
| Parallelism | Many operations executing at the same instant | Yes                   | `multiprocessing`, `ProcessPoolExecutor`, sub-interpreters, free-threaded threads |
| Asynchrony  | Waiting without blocking a thread             | No                    | `async` / `await` (`asyncio`)                         |

Parallelism is a *kind* of concurrency. Asynchrony is a *way* to achieve concurrency cheaply.

### 1.2 CPU-bound vs I/O-bound

This is the single most important question to ask before choosing a tool.

```
CPU-bound  : the work keeps a core busy the whole time
             e.g. image processing, hashing, parsing, pure-Python number crunching
             → more cores help → use PARALLELISM (processes / interpreters)

I/O-bound  : the work mostly WAITS for something external
             e.g. HTTP calls, database queries, disk reads, timers
             → a waiting thread does nothing → use ASYNCHRONY (asyncio) or threads
```

### 1.3 Python's twist: the GIL

The standard interpreter (CPython) has historically had a **Global Interpreter Lock (GIL)**: a mutex that lets only **one thread execute Python bytecode at a time** (per interpreter).

```
GIL build (the default python3.x):
  Thread 1:  [py][py]........[py]........[py]
  Thread 2:  ........[py]..........[py].......    only ONE runs Python at a time
  Thread 3:  [~~~~ waiting on I/O ~~~~][py]..     waiting on I/O RELEASES the GIL

Free-threaded build (python3.14t, python3.15t):
  Thread 1:  [py][py][py][py][py]
  Thread 2:  [py][py][py][py][py]                 truly parallel Python threads
```

The GIL is **released** during blocking I/O, `time.sleep`, and inside many C extensions doing heavy work (NumPy, `hashlib`, `zlib`, ...). That explains the classic consequences:

| Work                                       | Threads on GIL build        | Threads on free-threaded build | Processes / sub-interpreters |
| ------------------------------------------ | --------------------------- | ------------------------------ | ---------------------------- |
| I/O-bound (network, disk, DB)              | ✅ scales (GIL released)     | ✅ scales                       | ✅ but overkill               |
| CPU-bound **pure Python**                  | ❌ no speedup (takes turns)  | ✅ scales across cores          | ✅ scales across cores        |
| CPU-bound in a C extension that releases the GIL (NumPy) | ✅ often scales | ✅ scales                  | ✅ scales                     |

**Free-threading timeline:**

| Version | Status                                                                                       |
| ------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 3.13    | Experimental free-threaded build (PEP 703)                                                   |
| 3.14    | Officially supported, but still an **optional** separate build (PEP 779)                     |
| 3.15    | Stable ABI for free-threaded C extensions (`abi3t`, PEP 803); official macOS installers include free-threading support by default |

```python
import sys
import sysconfig

sysconfig.get_config_var("Py_GIL_DISABLED")  # 1 on a free-threaded build, 0 otherwise
sys._is_gil_enabled()                        # (3.13+) is the GIL actually off right now?
```

> A free-threaded interpreter **re-enables the GIL at runtime** (with a warning) if you import a C extension that isn't marked free-threading-safe. Check with `sys._is_gil_enabled()`.

> **Key insight:** the GIL protects the **interpreter's internals**, not **your program's invariants**. `counter += 1` is still read-modify-write and can still race, with or without the GIL (see [§5](#5-hazards-of-shared-state)).

> **Rule of thumb:**
> I/O-bound → `asyncio` (or a thread pool if your libraries are blocking).
> CPU-bound → processes / sub-interpreters (or threads on a free-threaded build).
> *"asyncio when you can, threads when you must, processes for CPU."*

## 2. The Two Problems: Execution vs Coordination

Every concurrent program has to solve two separate problems.

```
                     Concurrent programming
                    ┌──────────┴──────────┐
       (A) EXECUTION                 (B) COORDINATION
   "How do I run many things?"   "How do they share safely?"
   ──────────────────────────    ─────────────────────────────
   threading.Thread              Lock / RLock
   multiprocessing.Process       Semaphore / BoundedSemaphore
   concurrent.interpreters       Event / Condition / Barrier
   concurrent.futures Executors  queue.Queue / asyncio.Queue
   asyncio (coroutines, Tasks)   Future (a one-shot result)
                                 threading.local / contextvars
```

- **Execution** tools *create* concurrency: they start work and schedule it.
- **Coordination** tools *control* concurrency: they decide who may proceed, who must wait, and how shared data stays consistent.

```
  Execution creates the traffic        Coordination controls the traffic
  ─────────────────────────────        ──────────────────────────────────
  threads, processes, tasks      ──►   traffic lights, gates, toll booths
```

Most concurrency bugs (races, deadlocks, corrupted state) are coordination bugs.

**Python-specific wrinkle — three parallel "worlds".** Most coordination primitives exist in *three flavors with the same names*. Pick the family that matches your execution model; never mix them.

```
 Execution world          Coordination family
 ───────────────          ───────────────────────────────────────────────
 threads            ──►   threading.*        (+ queue.Queue)
 asyncio tasks      ──►   asyncio.*          (asyncio.Lock, asyncio.Queue, ...)
 processes          ──►   multiprocessing.*  (+ Manager, shared_memory)
 sub-interpreters   ──►   concurrent.interpreters queues
```

---

## 3. The Execution Stack

Python concurrency has **two roads** that meet in the middle: the *async road* (one thread, cooperative switching at `await`) and the *worker road* (threads, interpreters, processes, switched by the OS). Modern code lives mostly in the upper layers.

```
 ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ High-level   TaskGroup, gather,                    │ Executor.map,            │
 │ patterns     as_completed, asyncio.Queue           │ as_completed             │
 ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
 │ ASYNC ROAD  (cooperative, ONE thread)              │ WORKER ROAD              │
 │                                                    │ (OS-scheduled)           │
 │ Language    async def / await                      │                          │
 │             (coroutines pause and resume)          │ concurrent.futures       │
 │                                                    │ Executor + Future:       │
 │ Scheduler   asyncio event loop + Task              │  ThreadPoolExecutor      │
 │             (selector: kqueue / epoll / IOCP)      │  InterpreterPoolExecutor │
 │             to_thread / run_in_executor ───────────┼─► ProcessPoolExecutor    │
 ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┤
 │ Workers     threading.Thread  │  concurrent.interpreters  │  multiprocessing  │
 ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ Runtime/OS  OS thread (shared memory)       │       OS process (isolated)     │
 └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        ▲ higher = easier, safer, preferred
        ▼ lower  = more control, more cost, rarely needed directly
```

The three worker types sit on an **isolation spectrum**:

```
            Thread                 Sub-interpreter          Process
   ┌──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┐
   │ threading            │ concurrent.          │ multiprocessing      │
   │ ThreadPoolExecutor   │   interpreters (3.14)│ ProcessPoolExecutor  │
   │                      │ InterpreterPool-     │                      │
   │                      │   Executor (3.14)    │                      │
   ├──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
   │ Memory: SHARED       │ Same process, but    │ SEPARATE memory      │
   │ objects directly     │ objects ISOLATED     │ objects ISOLATED     │
   │ GIL: one, shared*    │ GIL: one per interp. │ GIL: one per process │
   │ Start cost: tiny     │ Start cost: small    │ Start cost: large    │
   │ Data passing: free   │ Data: pickle/queues  │ Data: pickle/pipes   │
   └──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┘
   ◄── cheaper, more sharing, more race risk     more isolation, safer ──►
   * free-threaded build: no GIL, threads run Python in parallel
```

### 3.1 `threading.Thread` — the lowest level

```python
import threading


def greet(name: str) -> None:
    """Print a greeting from a worker thread."""
    print(f"Hello {name} from {threading.current_thread().name}")


t = threading.Thread(target=greet, args=("world",), name="worker-1")
t.start()
t.join()  # block until it finishes
```

- Each thread is a real OS thread with its own stack. Creating many is expensive.
- A raw `Thread` has **no return value**, and an exception inside it is only printed (via `threading.excepthook`); `join()` doesn't re-raise. → Prefer `ThreadPoolExecutor`, which gives you a `Future`.
- `daemon=True` threads are killed abruptly at interpreter exit (no cleanup). Use only for truly disposable background work.
- Use raw threads for rare cases such as a long-running dedicated loop (a poller, a GUI worker).

### 3.2 `multiprocessing` — separate processes for CPU work

Each process has its own interpreter, memory, and GIL, so CPU-bound Python code runs truly in parallel.

```python
import multiprocessing as mp


def square(x: int) -> int:
    """Square a number in a worker process."""
    return x * x


if __name__ == "__main__":  # REQUIRED with spawn / forkserver
    with mp.Pool(processes=4) as pool:
        print(pool.map(square, range(10)))
```

**How a child process starts** (the *start method*):

| Method       | How it works                                       | Default on                               |
| ------------ | -------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `spawn`      | Fresh interpreter; re-imports your main module     | macOS (since 3.8), Windows               |
| `forkserver` | Forks from a clean, single-threaded server process | Linux (since 3.14)                       |
| `fork`       | Copies the parent process as-is (fast)             | Linux before 3.14 — unsafe with threads  |

Requirements that follow from this:

- Guard the entry point with `if __name__ == "__main__":` — otherwise each spawned child re-runs your top-level code.
- Arguments and results are **pickled** across the process boundary: functions must be importable top-level functions (no lambdas, no nested functions), and big objects cost real time to copy.
- To share data, use message passing (`mp.Queue`, `mp.Pipe`) or, when needed, `mp.Manager`, `mp.Value` / `mp.Array`, or `multiprocessing.shared_memory`.

In new code, prefer the higher-level `ProcessPoolExecutor` (next section). `mp.Pool` is still fine and offers extras like `imap_unordered` and `starmap`.

### 3.3 `concurrent.futures` — Executors and Futures (the "thread pool" layer)

An **Executor** is a pool of reusable workers; `submit()` returns a **Future**, a placeholder for a result that arrives later. All three executors share **one interface**, so the execution strategy is swappable (Strategy pattern / dependency inversion):

```python
import math
from concurrent.futures import (
    Executor,
    InterpreterPoolExecutor,  # 3.14+
    ProcessPoolExecutor,
    ThreadPoolExecutor,
)


def is_prime(n: int) -> bool:
    """Check primality by trial division (CPU-bound)."""
    if n < 2:
        return False
    return all(n % d for d in range(2, math.isqrt(n) + 1))


def count_primes(executor: Executor, numbers: range) -> int:
    """Count primes using whatever execution strategy is injected."""
    return sum(executor.map(is_prime, numbers, chunksize=1_000))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    numbers = range(10_000_000, 10_200_000)
    with ProcessPoolExecutor() as pool:        # CPU-bound → processes
        print(count_primes(pool, numbers))
```

```python
# I/O-bound with a blocking library → threads
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8) as pool:
    futures = {pool.submit(download, url): url for url in urls}
    for fut in as_completed(futures):          # completion order
        print(futures[fut], len(fut.result()))  # result() re-raises worker errors
```

| API                                              | Purpose                                                         |
| ------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `executor.submit(fn, *args)` → `Future`          | Schedule one call                                               |
| `executor.map(fn, iterable, chunksize=…)`        | Results **in input order**; `chunksize` matters for processes   |
| `executor.map(..., buffersize=N)` *(3.14+)*      | Bound how many tasks are queued ahead (huge/infinite inputs)    |
| `as_completed(futures)`                          | Iterate futures **in completion order**                         |
| `wait(futures, return_when=FIRST_COMPLETED)`     | Lower-level: returns `(done, not_done)` sets                    |
| `future.result(timeout=…)`                       | Block for the result; re-raises the worker's exception          |
| `future.cancel()`                                | Cancel — only works if it hasn't **started** yet                |
| `executor.shutdown(wait=True, cancel_futures=True)` | Stop accepting work; drop pending items *(3.9+)*             |

Defaults *(3.13+)*: `ThreadPoolExecutor` uses `min(32, os.process_cpu_count() + 4)` workers; `ProcessPoolExecutor` uses `os.process_cpu_count()`.

> **Pool starvation** exists here too: if pool workers *block waiting for other tasks in the same pool* (e.g. a task calls `submit(...).result()` on its own pool), the pool can deadlock. Don't wait on a pool from inside that pool.

### 3.4 Sub-interpreters — `concurrent.interpreters` *(3.14+)*

Multiple isolated interpreters inside **one process**, each with its own GIL. Think "processes, but lighter".

```python
import math
from concurrent import interpreters


def area(r: float) -> float:
    """Compute a circle's area."""
    return math.pi * r * r


if __name__ == "__main__":
    interp = interpreters.create()
    interp.exec("x = 21 * 2; print('inside:', x)")   # run source code
    print(interp.call(area, 2.0))                     # call a function, get a result

    queue = interpreters.create_queue()               # cross-interpreter queue
    interp.prepare_main(q=queue)
    interp.exec("q.put('hello via queue')")
    print(queue.get())
    interp.close()
```

- Objects are **not shared**; data crosses via queues or pickling — same mental model as processes.
- Like `spawn`, the worker may re-import `__main__`, so keep the `if __name__ == "__main__":` guard.
- Most code should use `InterpreterPoolExecutor` (same API as the other executors) rather than managing interpreters by hand.
- Many third-party C extensions don't support sub-interpreters yet; check before relying on them.

### 3.5 `asyncio` — coroutines on an event loop

#### Coroutine vs Task: "cold" vs "scheduled"

```python
coro = fetch("a")                  # nothing runs yet — just a coroutine object ("cold")
task = asyncio.create_task(coro)   # scheduled: starts at the next loop iteration
result = await task                # suspend until the task finishes
```

> **A coroutine is not a thread.** Thousands of tasks can share **one** thread; a task that is waiting on I/O costs a few KB of memory and no thread at all.

#### The event loop

```
 ┌──────────────────────── Event loop (ONE thread) ─────────────────────────┐
 │                                                                          │
 │   ready queue:  [Task A] [Task C] [callback] ...                         │
 │        │                                                                 │
 │        ▼ run each one until it hits an `await` that must wait            │
 │   Task A ── await reader.read() ──► register socket with the OS selector │
 │                                     (kqueue on macOS, epoll on Linux)    │
 │        ...loop runs Task C meanwhile...                                  │
 │   OS: "socket readable" ──► Task A goes back into the ready queue        │
 │                                                                          │
 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

#### What `await` actually does

```
async def get_report() -> str:
    validate()                    ── runs synchronously inside the current Task

    data = await load()           ── if load() can't finish immediately:
                                       1. the Task SUSPENDS (its frame is saved)
                                       2. control returns to the EVENT LOOP
                                       3. the loop runs other ready Tasks
                                       4. when the I/O completes, the loop
                                          resumes this Task right here

    return format_report(data)    ── resumes on the SAME thread (the loop's)
```

Two big consequences:

1. **Switching only happens at `await`.** Code between two `await`s runs without interruption by other tasks. This makes many races impossible — but a check before an `await` and an update after it can still race (see [§5.1](#51-race-condition)).
2. **Anything that blocks (without `await`) freezes every task.** `time.sleep(1)`, `requests.get(...)`, or a 2-second CPU loop inside `async def` stops the whole loop.

#### Running asyncio

```python
import asyncio


async def main() -> None:
    """Program entry point for async code."""
    ...


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())  # creates the loop, runs main(), closes the loop
```

Inside coroutines, use `asyncio.get_running_loop()` when you need the loop (`get_event_loop()` raises if no loop is running *(3.14+)*). In Jupyter, a loop is already running: use top-level `await main()` instead of `asyncio.run`.

#### Useful combinators

| API                                              | Purpose                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:` *(3.11+)* | **Structured concurrency**: wait for all; first failure cancels siblings |
| `await asyncio.gather(*aws)`                     | Wait for all; results **in input order**                                 |
| `asyncio.as_completed(aws)`                      | Handle results **in completion order** (`async for` *3.13+*)             |
| `await asyncio.wait(aws, return_when=…)`         | Lower-level: returns `(done, pending)`                                   |
| `async with asyncio.timeout(s):` *(3.11+)*       | Deadline for a block → `TimeoutError`                                    |
| `await asyncio.wait_for(aw, s)`                  | Timeout for a single awaitable                                           |
| `await asyncio.sleep(s)`                         | Asynchronous wait (no thread blocked)                                    |
| `await asyncio.shield(aw)`                       | Protect an inner operation from outer cancellation                       |
| `await asyncio.to_thread(fn, *args)` *(3.9+)*    | Run a **blocking** function in the default thread pool                   |
| `tg.cancel()` *(3.15+)*                          | Stop a `TaskGroup` early, without raising                                |

```python
import asyncio


async def fetch(url: str, delay: float = 0.1) -> str:
    """Pretend to download a URL."""
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    return f"<html of {url}>"


async def main() -> None:
    """Show TaskGroup and as_completed."""
    # Preferred: structured concurrency — no task can outlive this block
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        t1 = tg.create_task(fetch("a"))
        t2 = tg.create_task(fetch("b"))
    print(t1.result(), t2.result())

    # Handle results as soon as each finishes (3.13+)
    tasks = [asyncio.create_task(fetch(u, d)) for u, d in [("slow", 0.3), ("fast", 0.1)]]
    async for done in asyncio.as_completed(tasks):
        print(await done)  # fast first, then slow


asyncio.run(main())
```

#### Golden rules of asyncio

1. **Async all the way.** Never call blocking functions inside `async def`. Use async libraries (`httpx`, `aiohttp`, `asyncpg`, ...) or offload with `asyncio.to_thread`.
2. **Always `await` (or keep a reference).** A coroutine that's never awaited never runs (`RuntimeWarning: coroutine ... was never awaited`). The loop holds only *weak* references to tasks, so a fire-and-forget `create_task()` can vanish mid-flight. Prefer `TaskGroup`.
3. **One entry point.** Call `asyncio.run(main())` once, at the top. Don't nest it.
4. **Never swallow `CancelledError`.** Clean up in `finally`, then let it propagate (see [§7](#7-cancellation-and-timeouts)).
5. **Async iteration and resources:** async generators + `async for`, async context managers + `async with`.

```python
from collections.abc import AsyncIterator


async def paginate(client: ApiClient) -> AsyncIterator[Item]:
    """Yield items page by page without blocking the loop."""
    page = 1
    while batch := await client.get_page(page):
        for item in batch:
            yield item
        page += 1


async for item in paginate(client):
    process(item)
```

### 3.6 Bridging the two roads (sync ↔ async)

| I am in...           | ...and need to run                  | Use                                                            |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `async def`          | a blocking sync function (I/O)      | `await asyncio.to_thread(fn, *args)`                           |
| `async def`          | CPU-heavy sync function             | `await loop.run_in_executor(process_pool, fn, *args)`          |
| sync code (no loop)  | async code                          | `asyncio.run(main())` — once, at the entry point               |
| another thread       | a coroutine on a running loop       | `asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(coro, loop)` → `concurrent.futures.Future` |
| another thread       | a plain callback on a running loop  | `loop.call_soon_threadsafe(callback, *args)`                   |
| `async def`          | await a `concurrent.futures.Future` | `await asyncio.wrap_future(fut)`                               |

```python
import asyncio
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor


def crunch(n: int) -> int:
    """CPU-heavy work that would block the event loop."""
    return sum(i * i for i in range(n))


async def main() -> None:
    """Offload CPU work to processes, blocking I/O to threads."""
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    with ProcessPoolExecutor() as pool:
        total = await loop.run_in_executor(pool, crunch, 10_000_000)
    print(total)
    text = await asyncio.to_thread(read_big_file, "data.csv")  # any blocking function


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

> asyncio objects (`Task`, `asyncio.Lock`, `asyncio.Queue`, ...) are **bound to their loop and not thread-safe**. Cross the thread boundary only through the `*_threadsafe` APIs above.

### 3.7 High-level patterns

**Producer / consumer with a bounded queue** — the Python counterpart of a channel:

```
 Producer(s) ──await put()──► [ asyncio.Queue(maxsize=10): ▓▓▓▓░░ ] ──await get()──► Consumer(s)
                               if full, producers wait (backpressure)
                               queue.shutdown() → consumers get QueueShutDown (3.13+)
```

```python
import asyncio


async def producer(queue: asyncio.Queue[int]) -> None:
    """Put items, then signal 'no more items'."""
    for i in range(100):
        await queue.put(i)  # waits if the queue is full
    queue.shutdown()        # (3.13+) consumers drain the rest, then stop


async def consumer(name: str, queue: asyncio.Queue[int]) -> None:
    """Process items until the queue is shut down and empty."""
    while True:
        try:
            item = await queue.get()
        except asyncio.QueueShutDown:
            return
        print(f"{name} processed {item}")
        queue.task_done()


async def main() -> None:
    """Wire one producer to three consumers."""
    queue: asyncio.Queue[int] = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=10)
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        tg.create_task(producer(queue))
        for n in range(3):
            tg.create_task(consumer(f"c{n}", queue))


asyncio.run(main())
```

The thread version is identical in shape: `queue.Queue(maxsize=10)`, `q.put()` / `q.get()`, `q.shutdown()` *(3.13+)*, `queue.ShutDown`. For processes use `multiprocessing.Queue`.

**Sharing one iterator across threads** *(3.15+)*: a plain generator isn't thread-safe (`ValueError: generator already executing`). Wrap it:

```python
import threading

events = threading.serialize_iterator(stream_events())   # each item goes to ONE consumer
a, b = threading.concurrent_tee(stream_events(), n=2)     # every consumer sees EVERY item
```

**Multi-stage pipelines:** chain stages with queues (stage 1 → queue → stage 2 → queue → ...), each stage with its own number of workers. For larger data pipelines, look at third-party tools (Dask, Ray, joblib).

---

## 4. Choosing an Execution Model

```
What kind of work is it?
│
├─ I/O-bound (waiting on network / disk / DB)
│   ├─ Async library available (httpx, aiohttp, asyncpg, ...)?
│   │   ├─ One operation ......................... await it
│   │   ├─ Many, all at once (small N) ........... TaskGroup / gather
│   │   ├─ Many, but at most N at a time ......... asyncio.Semaphore + TaskGroup
│   │   └─ Continuous stream of work ............. asyncio.Queue (producer/consumer)
│   └─ Only a blocking library (requests, many DB drivers)?
│       ├─ From sync code ........................ ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=N)
│       └─ From async code ....................... await asyncio.to_thread(...)
│
└─ CPU-bound (keeps a core busy)
    ├─ Can it be vectorized (NumPy / pandas / polars)? ... do that FIRST
    ├─ Pure Python over a collection ............. ProcessPoolExecutor.map(chunksize=...)
    ├─ Same, lighter weight (3.14+) .............. InterpreterPoolExecutor
    ├─ On a free-threaded build (3.14t+) ......... ThreadPoolExecutor scales too
    └─ From async code ........................... await loop.run_in_executor(process_pool, ...)
```

| Scenario                                          | Use                                                          |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Call a web API from async code                    | `await client.get(...)` (`httpx.AsyncClient`)                |
| Download 200 files, max 5 at a time               | `asyncio.Semaphore(5)` + `TaskGroup`                         |
| Same, but only `requests` is available            | `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=5).map(...)`                 |
| Resize 10,000 images on all cores                 | `ProcessPoolExecutor().map(resize, paths, chunksize=50)`     |
| Keep a GUI / event loop responsive during heavy work | `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` or `run_in_executor(process_pool, ...)` |
| Background worker processing a queue of jobs      | `asyncio.Queue` (async) / `queue.Queue` (threads)            |
| Web server (FastAPI, etc.) calling a database     | `await` an async driver; don't wrap it in threads            |
| Heavy NumPy math on large arrays                  | Vectorize; NumPy releases the GIL internally                 |

---

## 5. Hazards of Shared State

When concurrent operations touch the **same data**, things go wrong in a few classic ways.

### 5.1 Race condition

The result depends on the unpredictable timing of operations. `counter += 1` looks like one step, but it is really three: read, add, write.

```
Thread A: read 5 ──────── add 1 ── write 6
Thread B:      read 5 ── add 1 ── write 6     ← one increment is lost
```

Try it yourself (save as `race.py`, run with `python race.py`):

```python
import threading
import time

N_THREADS, N_ITER = 8, 1_000
unsafe_count = 0
safe_count = 0
lock = threading.Lock()


def unsafe_work() -> None:
    """Increment without a lock: read-modify-write races."""
    global unsafe_count
    for _ in range(N_ITER):
        current = unsafe_count       # 1. read
        time.sleep(0)                # (invite a thread switch here)
        unsafe_count = current + 1   # 2-3. add + write


def safe_work() -> None:
    """Increment under a lock: always correct."""
    global safe_count
    for _ in range(N_ITER):
        with lock:
            current = safe_count
            time.sleep(0)
            safe_count = current + 1


for target in (unsafe_work, safe_work):
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=target) for _ in range(N_THREADS)]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join()

print(f"unsafe: {unsafe_count:,}")  # e.g. 1,003 (varies every run)
print(f"safe:   {safe_count:,}")    # 8,000
```

> Why the `time.sleep(0)`? On GIL builds since 3.10, threads switch less often, so a plain `counter += 1` loop may *look* correct on your machine. It is still not atomic: it races on free-threaded builds, under load, or after an innocent refactor. Never rely on luck.

**asyncio has races too** — not between bytecodes, but across an `await`:

```python
import asyncio

balance = 100


async def withdraw(amount: int) -> None:
    """Check-then-act across an await: races."""
    global balance
    if balance >= amount:        # check
        await asyncio.sleep(0)   # ← another task may run here
        balance -= amount        # act


async def main() -> None:
    """Two withdrawals of 100 from a balance of 100."""
    await asyncio.gather(withdraw(100), withdraw(100))
    print(balance)  # -100  ← both passed the check


asyncio.run(main())
```

Fix: wrap check-and-act in `async with lock:` using an `asyncio.Lock`. Or avoid the `await` between the check and the update — code without an `await` can't be interleaved by other tasks.

### 5.2 Deadlock

Two (or more) operations each wait for something the other holds, so none can continue.

```
Operation A holds lock1, wants lock2  ──┐
                                        ├── both wait forever
Operation B holds lock2, wants lock1  ──┘
```

Python-flavored ways to deadlock yourself:

- Re-acquiring a `threading.Lock` (or an `asyncio.Lock`) you already hold — neither is re-entrant.
- Calling `future.result()` on a pool from a task running *inside the same pool*.
- Holding a `threading.Lock` across an `await` (another task on the same loop then blocks the loop thread trying to take it).
- `os.fork()` while other threads hold locks: the child inherits locked locks with no owner (why `fork` is no longer the Linux default, *3.14+*).

Prevention:

- Always acquire multiple locks in the **same order**.
- Keep critical sections **small**; never call unknown code (callbacks, user hooks) while holding a lock.
- Use timeouts: `lock.acquire(timeout=5)`, `q.get(timeout=5)`, `async with asyncio.timeout(5):`.
- Never block on async code from inside the event loop.

### 5.3 Other hazards

| Hazard              | What happens                                                                                           |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Starvation          | Some work never gets a turn. In asyncio: one task blocks the loop and **every** other task starves     |
| Livelock            | Operations keep reacting to each other but make no progress                                            |
| Broken invariants   | A reader sees an object half-updated (`x` changed, `y` not yet). Each assignment is atomic; the *pair* isn't |
| Visibility          | Python has no formal memory model: publish data between threads through `Lock`, `Event`, or `Queue`, not ad-hoc flag variables |
| Pickling overhead   | With processes, copying big inputs/outputs can cost more than the computation itself                   |

### 5.4 What is (and isn't) safe with built-in types

Single operations on built-ins won't corrupt the object (the GIL, or per-object locks on free-threaded builds, protect it). **Compound** operations are a different story.

| Operation                                                    | Safe across threads?                                          |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `lst.append(x)`, `d[k] = v`, `d.get(k)` — one operation      | ✅ Won't corrupt the object                                    |
| `counter += 1`, `d[k] += 1`                                  | ❌ Read-modify-write races                                     |
| `if k not in d: d[k] = make()`                               | ❌ Check-then-act races (may run `make()` twice)               |
| Iterating a list/dict while another thread mutates it        | ❌ `RuntimeError` or skipped items                             |
| Sharing one generator/iterator across threads                | ❌ `ValueError: generator already executing` → `threading.serialize_iterator` *(3.15+)* |
| `queue.Queue`, `collections.deque` `append` / `popleft`      | ✅ Designed for it                                             |
| `asyncio.Queue` / `asyncio.Lock` from **another thread**     | ❌ Loop-bound; use `call_soon_threadsafe`                      |

> Assume a type is **not** safe for concurrent use unless its docs say otherwise.

---

## 6. The Coordination Toolbox

### 6.1 Map of the toolbox

Grouped by the *problem* each tool solves, from simplest (top) to most involved (bottom):

```
Coordination primitives
│
├─ Avoid sharing at all (best option when possible)
│     return values instead of mutating, tuple / frozenset / frozendict (3.15),
│     @dataclass(frozen=True), message passing (queue.Queue / asyncio.Queue)
│
├─ Per-context state (share nothing by design)
│     threading.local, contextvars.ContextVar  ◄── async-aware
│
├─ Thread-safe data structures
│     queue.Queue / LifoQueue / PriorityQueue / SimpleQueue, collections.deque
│
├─ Mutual exclusion  (only 1 at a time)
│     threading.Lock, threading.RLock (re-entrant),
│     multiprocessing.Lock (cross-process),
│     asyncio.Lock  ◄── async-capable
│
├─ Counting / limiting  (at most N at a time)
│     threading.(Bounded)Semaphore, multiprocessing.Semaphore,
│     Executor(max_workers=N),
│     asyncio.(Bounded)Semaphore  ◄── async-capable
│
├─ Waiting for a condition  ("sleep until this predicate is true")
│     threading.Condition, asyncio.Condition
│
├─ Signaling  ("wait until something happens")
│     threading.Event, threading.Barrier,
│     asyncio.Event, asyncio.Barrier (3.11),
│     asyncio.Future / concurrent.futures.Future  ◄── one-shot result
│
└─ Rate limiting  (at most X per time window)
      no stdlib tool → third-party (aiolimiter, limits) or a small token bucket
```

### 6.2 Same names, three worlds

| Primitive        | `threading` (blocks a thread)   | `asyncio` (awaits; loop-bound)      | `multiprocessing` (cross-process) |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Lock             | `Lock`, `RLock`                 | `Lock` (not re-entrant)             | `Lock`, `RLock`                   |
| Semaphore        | `Semaphore`, `BoundedSemaphore` | `Semaphore`, `BoundedSemaphore`     | `Semaphore`, `BoundedSemaphore`   |
| Event            | `Event`                         | `Event`                             | `Event`                           |
| Condition        | `Condition`                     | `Condition`                         | `Condition`                       |
| Barrier          | `Barrier`                       | `Barrier` *(3.11+)*                 | `Barrier`                         |
| Queue            | `queue.Queue`                   | `asyncio.Queue`                     | `multiprocessing.Queue`           |
| One-shot result  | `concurrent.futures.Future`     | `asyncio.Future`                    | (via `Pool` / `Executor`)         |
| Context-local    | `threading.local`               | `contextvars.ContextVar`            | — (separate memory anyway)        |

> **Key insight:** a `threading.Lock` inside `async def` blocks the **whole event loop**; an `asyncio.Lock` touched from another thread is **unsafe**. Pick the family that matches the execution model.

### 6.3 Avoid sharing (the best synchronization is none)

- Give each worker **its own data**, then combine results at the end (map → reduce).
- Use **immutable** objects (`tuple`, `frozenset`, `frozendict` *(3.15+)*, `@dataclass(frozen=True)`, `NamedTuple`): they can be shared freely because no one can change them.
- **Pass messages** instead of sharing memory: one worker owns the data, others send it requests through a queue.

```python
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor
from itertools import batched  # 3.12+


def chunk_sum(chunk: tuple[int, ...]) -> int:
    """Sum one chunk; touches no shared state."""
    return sum(chunk)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    numbers = range(10_000_000)
    with ProcessPoolExecutor() as pool:
        total = sum(pool.map(chunk_sum, batched(numbers, 100_000)))
    print(total)
```

### 6.4 Per-context state: `threading.local` and `contextvars`

When each thread or task needs its *own* copy of a "global" (request ID, DB session, locale), don't share — scope it.

```python
import asyncio
from contextvars import ContextVar

request_id: ContextVar[str] = ContextVar("request_id", default="-")


async def handle(rid: str) -> str:
    """Each task sees its own value, even across awaits."""
    request_id.set(rid)
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    return request_id.get()


async def main() -> None:
    """Two concurrent handlers don't see each other's request_id."""
    print(await asyncio.gather(handle("A"), handle("B")))  # ['A', 'B']


asyncio.run(main())
```

- `threading.local()` → one value **per thread**. Wrong tool for asyncio (all tasks share the loop thread).
- `ContextVar` → one value **per task** (each task copies the context when created); also works with threads and `to_thread`. This is what logging/tracing libraries use.

### 6.5 No `Interlocked`: a lock-protected counter

Python has no atomic-increment API. A small class with a `Lock` is the idiomatic answer — and it keeps the locking an internal detail (encapsulation):

```python
import threading


class AtomicCounter:
    """A counter that is safe to increment from many threads."""

    def __init__(self, start: int = 0) -> None:
        self._value = start
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def increment(self, by: int = 1) -> int:
        """Add `by` atomically and return the new value."""
        with self._lock:
            self._value += by
            return self._value

    @property
    def value(self) -> int:
        """Read the current value."""
        with self._lock:
            return self._value
```

If two fields must change together, put **both** updates inside the same `with self._lock:` block.

### 6.6 Thread-safe data structures (and the "factory runs twice" caveat)

- `queue.Queue` (FIFO), `LifoQueue`, `PriorityQueue`, `SimpleQueue`: blocking, thread-safe, with `maxsize` for backpressure.
- `collections.deque`: thread-safe `append` / `appendleft` / `pop` / `popleft` — a fast lock-free-feeling buffer.
- There is **no** `ConcurrentDictionary`. Use a `dict` + `Lock` for compound updates.

⚠️ **Caveat:** "get or create" helpers may build the value **more than once** under contention:

- `d.setdefault(k, expensive())` evaluates `expensive()` *every time*, even when the key exists.
- `functools.lru_cache` / `cache` are thread-safe internally, but the wrapped function **may run more than once** for the same key if calls overlap.

Thread version — double-checked locking:

```python
import threading

_cache: dict[str, Report] = {}
_lock = threading.Lock()


def get_report(report_id: str) -> Report:
    """Load each report at most once, even under concurrency."""
    if (report := _cache.get(report_id)) is not None:  # fast path, no lock
        return report
    with _lock:
        if (report := _cache.get(report_id)) is None:  # re-check under the lock
            report = _cache[report_id] = load_report(report_id)
        return report
```

asyncio version — cache the **in-flight task** (no lock needed, because there's no `await` between the check and the insert):

```python
import asyncio

_inflight: dict[str, asyncio.Task[Report]] = {}


async def get_report(report_id: str) -> Report:
    """Share one in-flight load per key among all callers."""
    task = _inflight.get(report_id)
    if task is None:
        task = _inflight[report_id] = asyncio.create_task(load_report(report_id))
    return await task
```

### 6.7 `Lock` / `RLock` — synchronous mutual exclusion

```python
import threading


class SafeList:
    """A list wrapper whose writes are serialized."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._lock = threading.Lock()   # private: outside code can't grab it
        self._items: list[int] = []

    def add(self, x: int) -> None:
        """Append under the lock."""
        with self._lock:
            self._items.append(x)

    def snapshot(self) -> list[int]:
        """Return a copy, so callers can iterate without holding the lock."""
        with self._lock:
            return list(self._items)
```

Rules:

- Always use `with lock:` — it releases even when an exception is raised.
- Keep the lock **private** to the object that owns the data. Don't lock on shared module-level objects other code might also use.
- Keep the critical section **short**; do slow work (I/O, heavy compute) outside it.
- `threading.Lock` is **not re-entrant**: acquiring it twice in the same thread deadlocks. Use `RLock` if a locked method calls another locked method (or better, restructure).
- **No `await` while holding a `threading.Lock`.** Use `asyncio.Lock` (`async with lock:`) in coroutines.
- Need a timeout? `lock.acquire(timeout=2)` returns `False` instead of waiting forever (if it returns `True`, release in a `finally`).

### 6.8 `Semaphore` — a gate with N slots

```
   asyncio.Semaphore(3)

   Waiting queue              Gate             Inside (critical section)
  ┌──────────────┐        ┌─────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ Task E       │        │ value=0 │        │ Task A  ── working   │
  │ Task D  ─────┼──────► │  ▓▓▓    │ ─────► │ Task B  ── working   │
  │ (awaiting)   │        │ (full)  │        │ Task C  ── working   │
  └──────────────┘        └─────────┘        └──────────┬───────────┘
         ▲                                              │
         │       Task A leaves `async with` (release)   │
         └────────── value 0→1, Task D enters ◄─────────┘
```

- `N = 1` → a lock. `N > 1` → a throttle.
- It's a **sliding window**, not batches: as soon as any slot frees up, the next waiter enters.
- Prefer `BoundedSemaphore`: an extra `release()` raises `ValueError` instead of silently growing the capacity.

```python
import asyncio


async def download(url: str, sem: asyncio.Semaphore) -> str:
    """Download with a concurrency cap."""
    async with sem:              # at most N bodies run here at once
        return await fetch(url)


async def download_all(urls: list[str], limit: int = 5) -> list[str]:
    """Download everything, never more than `limit` in flight."""
    sem = asyncio.BoundedSemaphore(limit)
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        tasks = [tg.create_task(download(u, sem)) for u in urls]
    return [t.result() for t in tasks]
```

> For 10,000 URLs this still creates 10,000 (cheap) task objects, only 5 of which do I/O at once. For truly huge inputs, use N worker tasks pulling from an `asyncio.Queue` instead ([§3.7](#37-high-level-patterns)).

### 6.9 `Condition` — wait until a predicate is true

Python has **no reader/writer lock** in the stdlib; a plain `Lock` is usually enough. What it *does* have is `Condition`: a lock plus "wake me when the state changes".

```python
import threading

items: list[int] = []
cond = threading.Condition()


def consumer() -> None:
    """Sleep until an item is available, then take it."""
    with cond:
        cond.wait_for(lambda: len(items) > 0)  # releases the lock while waiting
        print("got", items.pop())


def producer() -> None:
    """Add an item and wake one waiter."""
    with cond:
        items.append(42)
        cond.notify()
```

In practice, a `queue.Queue` covers most producer/consumer needs with less code. Reach for `Condition` for custom predicates.

### 6.10 Signaling — "wait until something happens"

| Primitive                                  | Behavior                                                         |
| ------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `threading.Event` / `asyncio.Event`        | A door: once `set()`, every waiter passes until `clear()`        |
| `threading.Barrier(n)` / `asyncio.Barrier(n)` | N participants wait for each other at each phase              |
| `concurrent.futures.Future`                | One-shot result for threads/processes (`set_result` / `result()`) |
| `asyncio.Future` (`loop.create_future()`)  | A one-shot awaitable you complete manually — the async-friendly signal |

`loop.create_future()` turns any callback or event into something you can `await`:

```python
import asyncio


async def main() -> None:
    """Await a value that some callback will deliver later."""
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    ready: asyncio.Future[str] = loop.create_future()

    # Somewhere else (a callback, a protocol, another task):
    loop.call_later(0.05, ready.set_result, "ready")
    # From ANOTHER THREAD use: loop.call_soon_threadsafe(ready.set_result, "ready")

    print(await ready)


asyncio.run(main())
```

### 6.11 Concurrency limit vs rate limit

```
Concurrency limit (Semaphore):   "at most 5 requests IN FLIGHT at once"
Rate limit:                      "at most 100 requests PER MINUTE"
```

The stdlib has no rate limiter. Use a third-party package (e.g. `aiolimiter` for asyncio, `limits` for general use), or write a small token bucket around `asyncio.sleep`.

---

## 7. Cancellation and Timeouts

Python has **three different cancellation models**, one per world:

```
asyncio    task.cancel() ──► CancelledError is RAISED INSIDE the task at its current `await`
           (injected)        the task may clean up (finally / except ... raise), then it ends

threads    no forced stop ──► cooperative flag: a threading.Event the loop checks regularly
           (cooperative)

processes  process.terminate() / kill(), ProcessPoolExecutor.terminate_workers() (3.14+)
           (forced)          no cleanup guaranteed — last resort
```

Unlike a token you must pass around, asyncio cancellation reaches **every** `await` automatically. The price: your code must **let `CancelledError` propagate**.

**asyncio — cancel with cleanup:**

```python
import asyncio


async def ticker() -> None:
    """Loop until cancelled, cleaning up on the way out."""
    try:
        while True:
            await asyncio.sleep(1)   # cancellation lands at an await
            print("tick")
    finally:
        print("cleaning up")         # runs on cancel, error, or normal exit


async def main() -> None:
    """Start a task, then cancel it."""
    task = asyncio.create_task(ticker())
    await asyncio.sleep(3.5)
    task.cancel()
    try:
        await task
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print("cancelled:", task.cancelled())  # True


asyncio.run(main())
```

**asyncio — timeouts** *(3.11+)*:

```python
async def load_all(files: list[str]) -> None:
    """Give the whole batch 10 seconds."""
    try:
        async with asyncio.timeout(10):        # cancels the block, raises TimeoutError
            async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
                for f in files:
                    tg.create_task(process(f))
    except TimeoutError:
        print("Timed out.")
```

**Threads — cooperative stop with `Event`:**

```python
import threading

stop = threading.Event()


def poll_server() -> None:
    """Poll every 30 s until asked to stop."""
    while not stop.is_set():
        check_server()
        stop.wait(30)  # sleeps, but wakes IMMEDIATELY when stop.set() is called


worker = threading.Thread(target=poll_server)
worker.start()
...
stop.set()      # request stop
worker.join()   # wait for it to finish cleanly
```

**Timeout APIs at a glance:**

| Where                       | API                                                   | On timeout                                     |
| --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| asyncio block               | `async with asyncio.timeout(s):` *(3.11+)*            | `TimeoutError` (inner work cancelled)          |
| asyncio single awaitable    | `await asyncio.wait_for(aw, s)`                       | `TimeoutError` (inner work cancelled)          |
| asyncio TaskGroup           | `tg.cancel()` *(3.15+)*                               | Group stops early, no exception                |
| `concurrent.futures.Future` | `fut.result(timeout=s)`                               | `TimeoutError` — **the work keeps running!**   |
| Thread                      | `t.join(timeout=s)` then `t.is_alive()`               | Returns; thread keeps running                  |
| Lock / queue                | `lock.acquire(timeout=s)`, `q.get(timeout=s)`         | `False` / `queue.Empty`                        |
| Executor shutdown           | `executor.shutdown(cancel_futures=True)` *(3.9+)*     | Pending (not started) items are dropped        |

Conventions:

- **Never swallow `CancelledError`.** Avoid bare `except:` and `except BaseException:` in coroutines. If you catch it for cleanup, re-raise it.
- Put cleanup in `finally` or `async with` — it runs on cancellation too.
- Use `asyncio.shield(aw)` for a short operation that must finish even if the caller is cancelled (e.g. committing a transaction).
- In thread workers, check a stop `Event` inside loops and long CPU work.

---

## 8. Exceptions in Concurrent Code

| Situation                                        | What you get                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `await task` / `await coro`                      | The **original** exception, with its traceback                                |
| `future.result()` (`concurrent.futures`)         | The worker's exception, **re-raised** in the caller                           |
| `executor.map(...)`                              | Raised when you **iterate** to the failed item; remaining results are lost    |
| `await asyncio.gather(...)`                      | The **first** exception propagates; the other tasks **keep running** (not cancelled) |
| `gather(..., return_exceptions=True)`            | Exceptions returned as **values** in the result list                          |
| `async with TaskGroup()`                         | Siblings are cancelled; **all** failures arrive in an `ExceptionGroup`        |
| A raw `threading.Thread` target raises           | Printed via `threading.excepthook`; `join()` does **not** raise; error is easy to miss |
| A task's exception is never retrieved            | Logged at garbage collection: *"Task exception was never retrieved"*          |
| A worker process dies abruptly                   | `BrokenProcessPool` (*3.15+* reports the PID and exit code)                   |

To see **all** failures, use `TaskGroup` + `except*` *(3.11+)*:

```python
import asyncio


async def might_fail(i: int) -> int:
    """Fail on odd numbers."""
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01 * i)
    if i % 2:
        raise ValueError(f"bad {i}")
    return i


async def main() -> None:
    """Handle failures from a group of tasks."""
    try:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
            for i in range(4):
                tg.create_task(might_fail(i))
    except* ValueError as eg:           # matches ValueErrors inside the group
        for exc in eg.exceptions:
            print("Failed:", exc)       # "bad 1" — task 3 was cancelled before it could fail


asyncio.run(main())
```

Or collect results and errors side by side with `gather(..., return_exceptions=True)`:

```python
results = await asyncio.gather(*(might_fail(i) for i in range(4)), return_exceptions=True)
# [0, ValueError('bad 1'), 2, ValueError('bad 3')]
ok = [r for r in results if not isinstance(r, BaseException)]
```

---

## 9. Common Pitfalls (and How to Debug Them)

| Pitfall                                                                 | Symptom                                                        | Fix                                                                  |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Blocking call in `async def`** (`time.sleep`, `requests.get`, heavy CPU) | Whole app freezes; every task stalls                          | `await asyncio.sleep`, async library, or `asyncio.to_thread`         |
| Forgetting `await`                                                      | Work never runs; `RuntimeWarning: coroutine ... was never awaited` | `await` it, or schedule it in a `TaskGroup`                      |
| Fire-and-forget `create_task()` without keeping a reference             | Task silently disappears mid-flight; errors lost               | `TaskGroup`, or store tasks in a set and discard on done             |
| Threads for CPU-bound pure Python (GIL build)                           | No speedup, sometimes slower                                   | `ProcessPoolExecutor` / `InterpreterPoolExecutor` / free-threaded build |
| Missing `if __name__ == "__main__":` with processes                     | `RuntimeError` at startup or endless child spawning (macOS/Windows) | Add the guard; keep worker functions at module top level        |
| Passing lambdas / local functions / open files to a process pool        | `PicklingError`                                                | Top-level functions; pass paths, not handles                         |
| Tiny tasks on a process pool                                            | Slower than serial (pickling dominates)                        | `chunksize=` in `map`, batch the work                                |
| Swallowing `CancelledError` (`except BaseException`, bare `except`)     | Tasks won't cancel; timeouts don't work; hung shutdown         | Catch specific exceptions; re-raise `CancelledError`                 |
| `asyncio.run()` inside a running loop (e.g. Jupyter)                    | `RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop` | Top-level `await`; one `asyncio.run` at the entry point |
| `threading.Lock` held across `await`                                    | Event loop deadlocks                                           | `asyncio.Lock`                                                       |
| Using asyncio objects from another thread                               | Random corruption / missed wakeups                             | `call_soon_threadsafe`, `run_coroutine_threadsafe`                   |
| Unbounded fan-out (`gather` over 10,000 HTTP calls)                     | Socket exhaustion, rate-limit bans, memory spikes              | `Semaphore`, bounded `Queue` + N workers, `max_workers`              |
| Check-then-act on a shared `dict`                                       | Duplicate work, overwritten values                             | Lock (double-checked), or cache in-flight tasks ([§6.6](#66-thread-safe-data-structures-and-the-factory-runs-twice-caveat)) |
| Re-acquiring a non-re-entrant `Lock`                                    | Deadlock                                                       | `RLock` (threads) or restructure (asyncio)                           |
| Waiting on a pool from inside the same pool                             | Pool deadlock                                                  | Don't nest; use separate pools or restructure                        |
| `fork` in a multi-threaded process                                      | Child hangs on an inherited lock (`DeprecationWarning` since 3.12) | `spawn` / `forkserver` start method                              |
| Relying on "it worked on my machine" for `counter += 1`                 | Rare, unreproducible wrong numbers in production               | Lock it; or don't share                                              |

### 9.1 Debugging tools

| Tool                                                         | What it shows                                                            |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `asyncio.run(main(), debug=True)` or `PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1`  | Never-awaited coroutines, callbacks that block the loop > 100 ms         |
| `python -X dev`                                              | Development mode: enables asyncio debug and extra runtime warnings       |
| `python -m asyncio ps <PID>` / `pstree <PID>` *(3.14+)*      | Live task list / await tree of a running asyncio program                 |
| `asyncio.print_call_graph()` *(3.14+)*                       | The await chain of the current task, from inside your code               |
| `faulthandler.dump_traceback_later(30)`                      | Stack of **every thread** if the program is still stuck after 30 s       |
| `profiling.sampling` (Tachyon) *(3.15+)*                     | Sampling profiler: `--async-aware` task stacks, `--mode gil` GIL holders |

---

## 10. Cheat Sheet

| I need to...                                         | Use                                                          |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Wait for I/O without blocking                        | `async` / `await` (`asyncio`)                                |
| Call a blocking function from async code             | `await asyncio.to_thread(fn, ...)`                           |
| Run blocking I/O concurrently from sync code         | `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=N)`                          |
| Process a collection on all cores (CPU, pure Python) | `ProcessPoolExecutor().map(fn, items, chunksize=...)`        |
| Same, lighter weight *(3.14+)*                       | `InterpreterPoolExecutor`                                    |
| Run CPU work from async code                         | `await loop.run_in_executor(process_pool, fn, ...)`          |
| Start several coroutines and wait for all            | `asyncio.TaskGroup` (or `gather`)                            |
| Handle results as each finishes                      | `asyncio.as_completed` / `concurrent.futures.as_completed`   |
| At most N async operations in flight                 | `asyncio.Semaphore(N)` (or N workers + `asyncio.Queue`)      |
| Producer/consumer queue                              | `asyncio.Queue` / `queue.Queue` / `multiprocessing.Queue`    |
| Increment a shared counter                           | A `Lock` (e.g. an `AtomicCounter` class)                     |
| Share a dictionary between threads                   | `dict` + `Lock` for compound updates                         |
| Protect a short synchronous block                    | `with threading.Lock():`                                     |
| Protect a block that contains `await`                | `async with asyncio.Lock():`                                 |
| Per-thread / per-task "globals"                      | `threading.local` / `contextvars.ContextVar`                 |
| Turn a callback into an awaitable                    | `loop.create_future()` + `set_result`                        |
| Stop a thread                                        | `threading.Event` checked in its loop                        |
| Stop async work on request or timeout                | `task.cancel()`, `asyncio.timeout(...)`                      |
| Share an iterator between threads *(3.15+)*          | `threading.serialize_iterator`                               |
| Coordinate across processes                          | `multiprocessing.Lock` / `Queue` / `Manager` / `shared_memory` |

**When multiple operations touch something shared, try these in order** (higher = simpler, fewer bugs):

```
1. Can I avoid sharing?               → return values, immutable data, queues
2. Is it per-thread / per-task state? → threading.local / ContextVar
3. Is it a stream of work?            → queue.Queue / asyncio.Queue
4. Short synchronous critical section? → threading.Lock (RLock only if re-entrant)
5. Does the block contain await?      → asyncio.Lock
6. Need "at most N at once"?          → Semaphore / Executor(max_workers=N)
7. Across processes?                  → multiprocessing primitives / Manager / shared_memory
```

---

## 11. The Big Picture

```
┌──────────────────────────────── CONCURRENT PROGRAMMING IN PYTHON ────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                                                  │
│   Ask first:  I/O-bound?  ──► ASYNCHRONY   asyncio (or threads for blocking libraries)           │
│               CPU-bound?  ──► PARALLELISM  processes, sub-interpreters, free-threaded threads    │
│                                                                                                  │
│   ┌───────────── (A) EXECUTION ──────────────┐     ┌──────────── (B) COORDINATION ────────────┐  │
│   │ ASYNC ROAD          │ WORKER ROAD        │     │ 1. Don't share  (immutable, queues)      │  │
│   │                     │                    │     │ 2. Scope it     (local, ContextVar)      │  │
│   │ TaskGroup, gather,  │ Executor.map,      │     │ 3. Queues       (queue / asyncio / mp)   │  │
│   │ asyncio.Queue       │ as_completed       │ ──► │ 4. Lock / RLock         (threads)        │  │
│   │        ▲            │        ▲           │     │ 5. asyncio.Lock         (await-safe)     │  │
│   │ async / await       │ Executor + Future  │     │ 6. Semaphore            (limit N)        │  │
│   │        ▲            │        ▲           │     │ 7. Event / Condition / Barrier / Future  │  │
│   │ event loop + Task ──┼─► Thread,          │     │ 8. Rate limiting        (third-party)    │  │
│   │ (one thread)        │   Interp., Process │     └──────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│   └──────────────────────────────────────────┘                                                   │
│                                                    Cross-cutting: the GIL (or free-threading),   │
│                                                    cancellation, ExceptionGroup, no blocking     │
│                                                    in the event loop                             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Five ideas to remember:**

1. **A coroutine is not a thread.** It doesn't even start until it's awaited or wrapped in a Task; a waiting task uses no thread at all.
2. **Classify the work first.** I/O-bound → asyncio (or threads). CPU-bound → processes / interpreters (or threads without the GIL).
3. **The GIL protects the interpreter, not your invariants.** Races still happen; coordinate explicitly.
4. **Execution creates concurrency; coordination keeps it correct.** And use the coordination family (`threading` / `asyncio` / `multiprocessing`) that matches your execution world.
5. **Never block the event loop; never swallow `CancelledError`.** Prefer `TaskGroup` so no task outlives its scope.

## 12. Further Reading

- **Python docs** — "asyncio — Asynchronous I/O" (especially *Coroutines and Tasks*, *Synchronization Primitives*, *Queues*, *Developing with asyncio*)
- **Python docs** — `concurrent.futures`, `threading`, `queue`, `multiprocessing`, `concurrent.interpreters` *(3.14+)*, `contextvars`
- **Python docs (HOWTO)** — "Python support for free threading"; **py-free-threading.github.io** (community guide for free-threaded builds and extensions)
- **PEPs** — PEP 703 (making the GIL optional), PEP 734 (multiple interpreters in the stdlib), PEP 654 (exception groups and `except*`)
- **Nathaniel J. Smith** — "Notes on structured concurrency, or: Go statement considered harmful" (the idea behind `TaskGroup`; see also Trio / AnyIO)
- **David Beazley** — "Python Concurrency From the Ground Up: LIVE!" (PyCon 2015 talk; builds threads → async from scratch)
- **Matthew Fowler** — *Python Concurrency with asyncio* (Manning)

## 13. Appendix: .NET → Python Rosetta Stone

| .NET                                          | Python                                                                |
| --------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Thread`                                      | `threading.Thread`                                                    |
| `ThreadPool`, `Task.Run(...)`                 | `ThreadPoolExecutor.submit(...)`, `asyncio.to_thread(...)`            |
| `Task<T>`                                     | `asyncio.Task` (async) / `concurrent.futures.Future` (pools)           |
| `async` / `await`                             | `async def` / `await`                                                 |
| `Task.WhenAll`                                | `asyncio.TaskGroup` / `asyncio.gather`                                |
| `Task.WhenAny`                                | `asyncio.wait(..., return_when=FIRST_COMPLETED)`                      |
| `Task.WhenEach` (.NET 9)                      | `asyncio.as_completed` (`async for`, 3.13+)                           |
| `Task.Delay`                                  | `asyncio.sleep`                                                       |
| `Parallel.ForEach`, PLINQ                     | `ProcessPoolExecutor.map` (CPU-bound, pure Python)                    |
| `Parallel.ForEachAsync` (max N)               | `asyncio.Semaphore(N)` + `TaskGroup`                                  |
| `Channel<T>`                                  | `asyncio.Queue` / `queue.Queue` (+ `shutdown()`, 3.13+)               |
| `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` + `await foreach`       | async generator + `async for`                                         |
| `lock` / `System.Threading.Lock`              | `with threading.Lock():`                                              |
| `SemaphoreSlim(1, 1)` (async lock)            | `asyncio.Lock`                                                        |
| `SemaphoreSlim(N, N)`                         | `asyncio.BoundedSemaphore(N)` / `threading.BoundedSemaphore(N)`       |
| `Interlocked`                                 | — (no equivalent; use a `Lock`)                                       |
| `ConcurrentDictionary`                        | — (`dict` + `Lock`)                                                   |
| `ConcurrentQueue`, `BlockingCollection`       | `queue.Queue`, `collections.deque`                                    |
| `ReaderWriterLockSlim`                        | — (no stdlib equivalent; `Lock` or `Condition`)                       |
| `ManualResetEventSlim`                        | `threading.Event` / `asyncio.Event`                                   |
| `Barrier`                                     | `threading.Barrier` / `asyncio.Barrier`                               |
| `TaskCompletionSource<T>`                     | `loop.create_future()`                                                |
| `CancellationToken`                           | `task.cancel()` (asyncio, injected) / `threading.Event` (threads)     |
| `CancelAfter`, `WaitAsync(timeout)`           | `asyncio.timeout(...)`, `asyncio.wait_for(...)`                       |
| `AggregateException`                          | `ExceptionGroup` + `except*`                                          |
| `ThreadLocal<T>`                              | `threading.local`                                                     |
| `AsyncLocal<T>`                               | `contextvars.ContextVar`                                              |
| `ConfigureAwait(false)`                       | — (not needed: no `SynchronizationContext`; resumes on the loop thread) |
| Named `Mutex` / `Semaphore`                   | `multiprocessing.Lock` / `Semaphore` (related processes only)         |

**Conceptual differences worth remembering:**

| Topic                  | .NET                                                  | Python                                                           |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Starting async work    | Calling an async method runs it until the first `await` ("hot") | Calling `async def` creates a coroutine that does nothing until awaited/scheduled ("cold") |
| Where code resumes     | Often a different thread-pool thread                  | Always the event loop's single thread                            |
| CPU parallelism        | Threads, out of the box                               | Processes / sub-interpreters, or threads on a free-threaded build |
| Cancellation           | Cooperative token you pass down explicitly            | asyncio: injected `CancelledError` at any `await`; threads: an `Event` flag |
| Primitives             | One set (with async-capable variants)                 | Three parallel families: `threading`, `asyncio`, `multiprocessing` |
